item.research_question: How do the electronic structure, thermal, magnetic, and mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) and conventional alloys (CAs) compare when varying composition across the transition from multi-principal element solid solutions to alloys dominated by one or two principal elements?
item.material_system: Cantor-type 3d transition metal alloys: (CrMnFeCo)1−xNix (0.2 ≤ x ≤ 0.92) and (CrMnCoNi)1−xFex (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.5); Quinary amorphous TE-TL alloys: (TiZrNbCu)1−xCox, (TiZrNbCu)1−xNix, and (TiZrNbNi)1−xCux
item.processing_route: Cantor-type alloys: High-frequency electromagnetic induction melting in water-cooled copper crucible under pure He, suction casting into 3 mm diameter cylinders, followed by annealing at 1373 K for 6 h under pure He; TE-TL alloys: Arc melting in high-purity argon with titanium getter, remelted five times, followed by melt spinning on a copper roller rotating at 25 m/s in pure helium to produce 25 μm thick ribbons
item.test_conditions: X-ray diffraction (Co-Kα, 0.178897 nm); Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) up to 1773 K at 20 K/min; Photoemission spectroscopy (UPS, He-I source, 21.2 eV, 25 meV resolution); Magnetic susceptibility (1.5–400 K and room temperature up to 1100 K); Nanoindentation (max load up to 12 mN, 300–400 nm depth); Microhardness (0.981 N load, 15 s); Young's modulus via ultrasonic velocity
key_findings: The experimental melting temperature (Tm) of (CrMnFeCo)1−xNix increases nonlinearly from 1563 K to 1728 K for pure Ni, whereas the rule of mixtures predicts a linear decrease from 1792 K.
In (TiZrNbCu)1−xNix amorphous alloys, the experimental Tm increases from 1121 K to 1179 K, while the rule of mixtures predicts a linear decrease from 2041 K to 1883 K.
The mixing enthalpy (∆Hmix) for (TiZrNbCu)1−xNix decreases rapidly from −6.6 kJmol−1 to −32 kJmol−1 at x = 0.5, whereas for (TiZrNbNi)1−xCux it increases nearly linearly from −28.2 to −15 kJmol−1.
Atomic size mismatch (δ) in Cantor-type alloys is small, around 1%, which is about ten times smaller than the δ values (8% to 10%) observed in the quinary TE-TL alloys.
The ratio Ω = ∆Sconf Tm/∆Hmix places all studied alloys above the region occupied by amorphous alloys when Tm is calculated by the rule of mixtures, leading to erroneous phase predictions.
The electronic density of states (DOS) in 3d transition metal CCAs shows a smooth variation with energy, contrasting with the split band shape of DOS in the TE-TL alloy family.
Thermal stability of conventional alloys (x ≥ 0.35) is better than that of high-entropy alloys in both the Cantor-type and quinary TE-TL systems.
Elemental distributions in all studied alloys were random down to the micrometer scale, with composition calculated from EDS at different locations being the same within about 1 at. %.
item.mechanism: The variations in intrinsic properties with composition mirror the evolution of the electronic structure; strong interatomic interactions in TE-TL alloys lead to a large negative ∆Hmix that outweighs the configurational entropy term (∆Sconf Tm), limiting the influence of entropy on phase formation, while the rule of mixtures fails because it does not account for these strong bonding tendencies and local atomic arrangements.
item.limitations: The study notes that the ∆Hmix−δ diagram is not sufficient for classifying alloys that can be prepared as metallic glasses depending on processing conditions, and that the rule of mixtures provides erroneous values for thermal parameters and phase predictions in both crystalline and amorphous HEAs.
item.future_work: The authors state that the complex crystallization processes in quinary TE-TL metallic glasses will make future studies of the evolution of crystallization products with composition and temperature much more complicated than those for corresponding binary metallic glasses.
quotes: The compositions of the alloys having the best properties depend on the alloy system and the property selected.
The rule of mixtures predicts a linear decrease in Tm from 1792 K for x = 0.2 towards that of pure Ni, whereas the experimental values increase nonlinearly from 1563 to 1728 K for pure Ni.

Since our as-cast alloy TiZrNbCu, in which ∆Sconf Tm (12.84 kJ/mole) considerably outweighs ∆Hmix (6.6 kJ/mole, Figure 2), ∆Sconf Tm/∆Hmix = 1.95, was multiphase (IM) [], it seems that in our alloys, configurational entropy has limited influence on the formation of either an SS or an amorphous phase.

item.research_question: How do thermal stability, glass-forming ability (GFA), atomic structure, electronic structure, and magnetic properties evolve during the transition from high-entropy alloys (HEAs) to conventional alloys (CAs) in quinary TE-TL metallic glasses, and what explains the discrepancy between good thermal stability and modest GFA?
item.material_system: (TiZrNbNi)1−xCux, (TiZrNbCu)1−xNix, (TiZrNbCu)1−xCox, and (CrMnFeCo)1−xNix alloys with x ranging from 0 to 1
item.processing_route: As-cast amorphous alloys and homogenized crystalline samples; annealing above Tx for structural analysis; High-energy XRD (HEXRD), UPS, XPS, Low-Temperature Specific Heat (LTSH), and Vickers microhardness measurements
item.test_conditions: Room temperature for hardness and magnetic susceptibility; 2 K for M-H data; DSC for thermal parameters (Tx, Tg, Tm, Tl); photon energy-dependent photoemission for electronic structure
key_findings: Thermal parameters (Tx, Tm, Tg) in (TiZrNbNi)1−xCux increase linearly for x ≤ 0.43 and decrease slightly at x = 0.5, unlike the quasi-linear behavior in binary TE-Cu MGs.

A crossover in intrinsic properties occurs at x ≈ 0.43 for Ni-containing alloys and x ≈ 0.25 for Co-containing alloys, coinciding with changes in atomic short-range order (SRO) and electronic structure.

The reduced glass transition temperature (Trg) and γ criterion erroneously predict low GFA at equiatomic compositions (x = 0.2) where experimental GFA is actually highest; using Tm instead of Tl in these criteria corrects the prediction.

The enthalpy of the last crystallization event (∆Hcl) shows a pronounced maximum around equiatomic composition, indicating the formation of a relatively stable phase, while the first event (∆Hcf) has small, non-trended values.

Average atomic packing fractions (APF) and coordination numbers (N) remain constant in (TiZrNbNi)1−xCux (ideal solution) but exhibit a sudden increase around x = 0.25 (Co) and x = 0.43 (Ni) in other systems.

Electronic density of states (DOS) shows a split valence band structure where d-states of transition elements (TE) dominate at low TL content, with a band crossing at elevated x causing a sharp increase in the Sommerfeld coefficient (γ) and magnetic susceptibility (χexp).
Magnetic susceptibility (χexp) decreases linearly in Cu-containing alloys but passes through a minimum and increases in Ni and Co alloys at the same crossover concentrations where APF and N change.
Vickers microhardness (HV) variations reflect subtle changes in local atomic arrangements, such as the increase in APF, and correlate with interatomic bonding strength.
item.mechanism: The transition from HEA to CA is driven by the evolution of the electronic structure (ES), specifically the shift of d-states of transition metals (TL) toward the Fermi level (EF), leading to band crossing. This electronic change alters the local atomic arrangements (increasing APF and N) and magnetic correlations, which in turn govern thermal stability and mechanical properties. The discrepancy between high thermal stability and low GFA arises because the first crystallization event (governing stability) and the last crystallization event (governing GFA via liquidus temperature) involve different phases and complex crystallization patterns.
item.limitations: The authors state that DSC peak overlaps make ∆Hc values inaccurate; simple XRD cannot provide direct insight into local atomic arrangements in amorphous alloys; non-spin-resolved UPS cannot provide full information on band structure and magnetic ground state; and the origin of magnetic clusters in some alloys is not yet clear.
item.future_work: XRD analysis of phases associated with each crystallization event is required for detailed insight; UPS and XPS studies with higher photon energies are needed to separate contributions of TE and TL states to the DOS; ab initio calculations are required to better understand the evolution of ES and magnetism in Cantor-type alloys.
quotes: Since the thermal stability of the same MG is associated with the separate first crystallization event (occurring around Tx), it may remain high, regardless of its low GFA.

Thus, knowledge of the evolution of the ES with the composition is perhaps the simplest way of predicting the change in intrinsic properties on the transition from the HEA to the CA concentration range.
